description: An evergreen shrub or small gnarled tree, usually one to three metres, of one to a few crooked stems and branches with grey-brown, shreddy bark, and small, thick, dark green leaves cut into a few narrow lobes and dotted with glands. In late spring it is covered with sweet-scented cream-white flowers a couple of centimetres across, then with seeds that each carry a long feathery plume. At the Grand Canyon it grows in the pinyon-juniper woodland below and along the rims, on dry, exposed ledges and cliffs, often of limestone, and is the main winter browse of mule deer on the Kaibab Plateau.

season_notes.winter: Dark green and leafy: the mule deer's main winter browse on the Kaibab Plateau; the old plumes are gone.
season_notes.spring: Flowering from April: a mass of fragrant cream-white, five-petalled flowers over the dark leaves.
season_notes.summer: Flowers keep coming after rain until frost; the feathery plumes of the seeds catch the light from July.
season_notes.fall: Plumed seeds blow away or are carried off and cached by rodents; the leaves stay dark green.

notes: Birchleaf mountain mahogany (the template) is the library's nearest hand-written Rosaceae shrub with small evergreen leaves and plumed seeds (curl-leaf mountain mahogany is a generated record and cannot be a template), but its leaves are toothed ovals, its bark smooth grey, its outline a clean upright vase, and it has no showy flowers. The card makes cliffrose a crooked, open shrub or small tree (Wikipedia: shrub 1-3 m, sometimes 4 m and somewhat treelike, rarely to 8 m; FEIS: 0.3-1.8 m usually, to 7.5 m on good sites, single- or many-stemmed), with shreddy bark (FEIS, Wikipedia), small thick lobed glandular leaves (Wikipedia; FEIS: small, evergreen, alternate to clustered, glandular), cream-white flowers (Wikipedia: white or cream, clawed petals, strongly sweet-scented, abundant, spring to first frost; FEIS: April-September in Arizona), and feathery seed plumes drawn through the berries block (FEIS: the plumed style 1-3.5 cm; Wikipedia: up to 6 cm; seeds ripening mid-July to August and shed into October in Utah). The template's oval leaf cards will look too broad and plain for the lobed leaves; the gnarled habit relies on the stems, lean and asymmetry here. Leaf size, flower size (and the five petals of a rose-family flower), the April-June main flowering span and the plume colour are the drafter's (no source read gives the sizes). Form: shrub, as the library's mountain mahoganies (the nearest relatives) are; multi_stem_shrub_tree is the other choice if the lineup wants the treelike old plants. Elevation: FEIS gives 914-2438 m in Arizona and 975-2745 m in Utah. Sites (FEIS): pinyon-juniper woodland, dry open ponderosa pine, mountain brush and desert shrubland edges, cliffs and dry exposed sites, mostly south- or west-facing and often on limestone; Wikipedia: often on cliffs, rocky soils, especially limestone. The Grand Canyon NPS pages read do not name cliffrose; FEIS reports it in Grand Canyon pinyon-juniper (a crown-fire study) and as the principal winter browse on the Kaibab Plateau. Fire: usually killed by severe fire, a weak sprouter, slow to return (FEIS: 13-15 years after a Grand Canyon crown fire far fewer plants on burned than unburned ground), so disturbed is low. Eaters (FEIS, Wikipedia): mule deer (important, heavy winter use), elk (browse and bedding cover), desert bighorn, pronghorn and livestock; rodents eat and cache the seeds; game birds and songbirds use it. Desert bighorn and pronghorn are not in the library; the deer mouse stands in for the seed-caching rodents. Colours, crown profile, porosity, stems, lean, habitat weights and the flower and plume blocks are the drafter's judgement, not from a source.
